headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA)
headings.content: Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) is a safe, highly effective, and widely utilized surgical procedure in reproductive healthcare, particularly relevant in resource-limited settings across Nigeria. Defined simply, MVA involves the evacuation of uterine contents using a specially designed handheld plastic syringe and a flexible or rigid cannula, creating a vacuum manually without requiring an electric suction machine or a large operating theatre setup. This procedure has revolutionized post-abortion care and the management of first-trimester pregnancy loss because it can be performed efficiently in outpatient clinics, reducing hospital stays and overall healthcare costs. For Nigerian nursing students, understanding MVA is vital as it bridges the gap between major surgical theatre interventions and bedside care. The MVA syringe is engineered to hold a vacuum of up to 660 mmHg, providing sufficient negative pressure to empty the uterine cavity gently and completely. Furthermore, MVA minimizes the risk of general anesthesia complications because it is frequently performed using paracervical block combined with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or conscious sedation. The World Health Organization endorses MVA as a preferred method for uterine evacuation up to 14 weeks of gestation, highlighting its safety profile, lower rates of uterine perforation compared to traditional sharp curettage, and high patient acceptance. Nurses play a crucial frontline role in identifying eligible patients, preparing the environment, assisting the clinician, and providing compassionate post-procedural support to ensure optimal maternal health outcomes.

headings.title: Indications and Contraindications for MVA
headings.content: Proper patient selection through clear indications and contraindications is a cornerstone of safe Manual Vacuum Aspiration practice. Indications for MVA include incomplete abortion, missed abortion or blighted ovum up to 14 weeks from the last menstrual period, elective first-trimester termination of pregnancy, and management of molar pregnancy when appropriate. Additionally, MVA is heavily utilized in post-abortion care (PAC) protocols across Nigerian hospitals to treat women presenting with incomplete miscarriages, significantly reducing maternal morbidity and mortality associated with hemorrhage and sepsis. Conversely, absolute and relative contraindications must be meticulously assessed by the healthcare team before scheduling the procedure. Absolute contraindications include a proven or strongly suspected intrauterine pregnancy beyond 14 weeks of gestation (due to increased risk of uterine perforation and severe hemorrhage), suspected or confirmed ectopic pregnancy, and severe, uncorrected coagulopathies. Relative contraindications encompass acute pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which should ideally be treated or concurrently managed with antibiotics, severe anatomical distortion of the cervix or uterus such as large fibroids, and acute systemic instability where stabilization must take priority over uterine evacuation. Nursing students must always review the patient's gestational age via clinical assessment and ultrasound, check vital signs, and screen for infections or bleeding disorders to ensure MVA is the appropriate and safest intervention for the individual client.

headings.title: Components of the MVA Instrument and Assembly
headings.content: Mastering the components of the Manual Vacuum Aspiration instrument and its correct assembly is a vital technical competency for nursing and midwifery students. The standard MVA kit comprises two main components: the vacuum syringe and the cannulae. The MVA syringe is typically a double-valve or single-valve plastic cylinder fitted with a plunger, a plunger rod, a collar stop, and button valves. The vacuum is created by pulling back the plunger until the arms of the plunger snap past the collar stop, locking it in place to maintain negative pressure until released by the operator. The cannulae are flexible or rigid plastic tubes (such as Karman cannulae) ranging in size from 4mm to 12mm, designed to match the estimated weeks of gestation and dilate the cervix minimally. Each cannula features lateral openings near the tip to maximize tissue aspiration while minimizing trauma to the myometrium. Before any procedure, the nurse must inspect all parts for cracks, wear, or leaks. Assembling the instrument requires ensuring the valves are functioning correctly, the O-ring is properly lubricated with a medical-grade silicone lubricant to maintain an airtight seal, and the plunger can be smoothly drawn back and locked. Testing the vacuum prior to insertion into the patient is mandatory; the nurse creates the vacuum in the syringe and leaves the pinchcock closed or the valves shut, handing it to the clinician only after confirming that the negative pressure holds steady without leaking air.

headings.title: Pre-Procedure Preparation and Patient Counseling
headings.content: Pre-procedure preparation and patient counseling form the bedrock of holistic, patient-centered nursing care in MVA services. When a patient presents for uterine evacuation, nurses must establish a therapeutic, empathetic rapport to alleviate the profound anxiety, fear, or grief often associated with pregnancy loss or termination. Comprehensive counseling involves explaining the MVA procedure in simple, local terminology, outlining what sensations to expect (such as strong menstrual-like cramps), discussing pain management options like a paracervical block, and addressing any misconceptions. Informed consent must be voluntary and obtained in accordance with legal and ethical standards in Nigeria. Physically preparing the patient involves conducting a baseline vital sign assessment, checking relevant laboratory results (such as hemoglobin, blood group, and rhesus factor), asking the patient to empty their bladder immediately before the procedure to reduce uterine displacement, and performing a focused bimanual pelvic examination to determine uterine size, position, and consistency. The nurse must also administer any prescribed prophylactic antibiotics or anti-anxiety medications as ordered by the clinician. Ensuring the procedure room is private, warm, and well-equipped with emergency resuscitation tools creates a safe environment. By addressing both the emotional and physical needs of the patient, the nurse significantly enhances coping mechanisms, promotes cooperation during the procedure, and fosters trust in the healthcare system.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Performing MVA
headings.content: Performing a Manual Vacuum Aspiration requires strict adherence to aseptic technique, precise anatomical knowledge, and coordinated teamwork between the clinician and the nursing assistant. The procedure begins with the patient in the lithotomy position. The vulva, perineum, and vagina are cleansed with an antiseptic solution (such as povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine), and sterile drapes are applied. A speculum is inserted to visualize the cervix, which is then cleansed again. If required, a local anesthetic like lidocaine is injected into the cervix to perform a paracervical block. The clinician gently grasps the anterior lip of the cervix with a tenaculum to straighten the uterocervical angle. Serial mechanical dilators are then introduced cautiously to dilate the cervical os just enough to accommodate the chosen cannula size, matching the weeks of gestation. Once dilated, the pre-assembled and tested MVA syringe containing a locked vacuum is connected to the cannula. The cannula is gently inserted through the internal os until it touches the uterine fundus, then withdrawn slightly. The pinchcock or valves on the syringe are released to activate the suction. The operator rotates the syringe 180 degrees in both directions while gently moving the cannula inward and outward from the internal os to the fundus, ensuring complete evacuation of all products of conception. Signs of a complete evacuation include a gritty feeling as the cannula passes over the surface, foam or tissue appearing in the transparent cannula without further blood, and the uterus contracting tightly around the cannula. Finally, the vacuum is released, the instruments are withdrawn, and the tissue is inspected for completeness before post-procedure monitoring begins.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Care and Monitoring
headings.content: Post-procedure care and monitoring are critical nursing responsibilities designed to ensure hemodynamic stability, detect early complications, and promote physical and emotional recovery. Immediately following MVA, the nurse transfers the patient to a recovery area and initiates vital sign monitoring (blood pressure, pulse, respiration, and temperature) every 15 minutes for the first hour, and then as clinically indicated. The nurse must closely monitor vaginal bleeding, checking sanitary pads for amount, color, and presence of clots, as well as assessing uterine tone to ensure the myometrium remains firmly contracted. Pain management is another key focus; nurses administer prescribed analgesics such as ibuprofen or paracetamol and offer emotional reassurance, recognizing the psychological impact of pregnancy loss or termination. Before discharge, nurses must provide comprehensive education covering warning signs (such as heavy bleeding soaking more than two pads per hour for two consecutive hours, severe lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge, or fever), hygiene instructions including avoiding vaginal douching and sexual intercourse for at least two weeks, and guidance on follow-up appointments. Contraceptive counseling and provision are also vital components of post-MVA care, as fertility can return as early as two weeks post-procedure. The nurse helps the client choose an appropriate method—such as pills, injectables, implants, or intrauterine devices—and ensures initiation before the patient leaves the health facility, thereby reducing the risk of unwanted repeat pregnancies.

headings.title: Recognition and Management of Complications
headings.content: Although Manual Vacuum Aspiration is exceptionally safe, nursing students must be vigilant in recognizing and managing potential complications promptly to prevent severe morbidity or mortality. Complications can be immediate, occurring during or right after the procedure, or delayed, presenting days later. Immediate complications include uterine perforation (often caused by the sound, dilator, or cannula), cervical laceration from the tenaculum, heavy hemorrhage due to uterine atony or retained products of conception, vasovagal reactions (manifested by bradycardia, hypotension, pallor, and sweating), and adverse reactions to local anesthetics. Delayed complications primarily involve pelvic infection (endometritis or pelvic inflammatory disease) and incomplete abortion presenting with persistent bleeding and cramping. When a complication arises, the nurse must act swiftly: for a vasovagal episode, elevate the patient's legs, apply cold compresses, and monitor vitals; for excessive bleeding, administer uterotonics such as oxytocin or misoprostol as ordered, check uterine tone, and notify the clinician immediately. If uterine perforation is suspected, the procedure must stop instantly, vital signs monitored, intravenous access secured, and the patient prepared for possible surgical exploration or laparoscopy if internal bleeding or organ damage is suspected. Documentation must be accurate, detailing the onset of symptoms, nursing actions taken, and the physician's response, reinforcing the nurse's role as a vital safety net in emergency response.

headings.title: Instrument Processing, Cleaning, and Sterilization
headings.content: Proper instrument processing, cleaning, and sterilization are critical components of infection prevention and control in any clinical setting performing Manual Vacuum Aspiration. Following the procedure, contaminated instruments—including syringes and cannulae—must undergo a standardized protocol to protect healthcare workers, patients, and the community from bloodborne pathogens like HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C. The decontamination process begins immediately after use by flushing the MVA syringe and cannulae with clean water to remove gross organic tissue and blood clots before the blood dries. Next, the instruments are thoroughly washed in a basin containing water and detergent, using a soft brush to scrub all surfaces, valves, and inner lumens of the cannulae. After washing, the items must be thoroughly rinsed with clean water and inspected for residual debris or structural damage. Depending on available hospital resources and manufacturer guidelines, instruments are then subjected to high-level disinfection (HLD) through boiling or chemical soaking, or complete sterilization using an autoclave. For MVA syringes, specific manufacturer instructions regarding heat tolerance must be followed; many modern plastic MVA syringes are autoclavable, while others require chemical HLD. Once processed and dried, instruments are stored in a clean, dry, dust-free environment until their next use. Nursing students must rigorously adhere to universal precautions, wear heavy-duty utility gloves during cleaning, and ensure strict compliance with institutional infection control policies to maintain a sterile continuum of care.
